main.title: Donkey Kong Jr.
main.summary: Donkey Kong Jr. is a 1982 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for arcades.

cards.text: Donkey Kong Jr. is a 1982 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for arcades. It is the sequel to 1981's Donkey Kong, but with the roles reversed compared to its predecessor: Mario is now the villain and Donkey Kong Jr. is trying to save his kidnapped father. After its initial release in arcades, the game was ported to a variety of home consoles, including the Famicom/Nintendo Entertainment System (for which the game was released as a launch title in Japan). The game's title is written as Donkey Kong Junior in the North American arcade version and various conversions to non-Nintendo systems.

The game was principally designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and his co-worker, Nintendo chief engineer Gunpei Yokoi. Miyamoto also created the graphics for the game along with Yoshio Sakamoto. As with its predecessor, the music for the game was composed by Yukio Kaneoka.
A sequel, Donkey Kong 3, and a spin-off game, Donkey Kong Jr. Math, were released in 1983.

main.title: Ms. Pac-Man
main.subtitle: The Sequel Born Outside the Maze
main.summary: Ms. Pac-Man reached the American public on 3 February 1982, bringing new mazes, moving fruit and altered ghost behaviour to the maze game.

cards.heading: The Sequel Born Outside the Maze
cards.text: Ms. Pac-Man is a 1982 arcade maze game developed from General Computer Corporation's Crazy Otto and released by Midway in North America. Presented to the American public on 3 February, it adds different mazes, moving fruit and less predictable ghost behaviour to the original Pac-Man rules. Its development began as an enhancement kit for existing cabinets before Midway turned it into an official sequel.

cards.heading: Before It Was a Sequel, It Was an Unauthorized Modification
cards.text: General Computer Corporation worked on Crazy Otto during summer 1981. The kit could modify an existing Pac-Man cabinet while retaining much of its hardware. An earlier dispute with Atari required GCC to obtain manufacturers' approval before selling further conversion kits. The team therefore took Crazy Otto to Midway, Pac-Man's North American distributor, which acquired the project and developed it into Ms. Pac-Man.

cards.heading: A Few Rule Changes Are Enough to Break Player Memory
cards.text: Four alternating mazes change the routes players can learn. Fruit moves through the playfield, while revised ghost behaviour makes a memorised pattern less dependable. Tunnel layouts and wall colours distinguish the stages. Players still collect dots and avoid or pursue ghosts, but need to keep reading the changing situation rather than rely entirely on the same sequence of movements.

cards.heading: A Visible Protagonist Also Changes the Conversation Around the Arcade
cards.text: Midway presented Ms. Pac-Man partly in response to the many women already playing Pac-Man. The sequel made a female protagonist the centre of a major arcade success. Its popularity also depended on the changes to the mazes and pursuit. In 2022, The Strong inducted the game into the World Video Game Hall of Fame, recognising its commercial reach and cultural significance.

main.title: Dig Dug
main.summary: Dig Dug is a 1982 maze video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: Drawing tunnels through the earth
cards.text: Dig Dug is a 1982 maze video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released by Atari, Inc. in North America. The player digs underground tunnels in each level to escape and attack enemy characters, by either inflating them to bursting or crushing them underneath rocks.

cards.heading: A movement jingle and a strategic pitch
cards.text: Dig Dug was planned and designed by Masahisa Ikegami with help from Galaga creator Shigeru Yokoyama. It was programmed for the Namco Galaga arcade board by Shouichi Fukatani, who worked on many of Namco's earlier arcade games, along with Toshio Sakai. Music was composed by Yuriko Keino, including the character movement jingle at executives' request, as her first Namco game. Namco heavily marketed it as a "strategic digging game".

cards.heading: Characters that outlive the cabinet
cards.text: Upon release, Dig Dug was well received by critics for its engaging gameplay and kawaii character design. During the golden age of arcade video games, it was globally successful, including as the second highest-grossing arcade game of 1982 in Japan. It prompted a long series of sequels and spin-offs, including the Mr. Driller series, for several platforms. It is in many Namco video game compilations for many systems.

main.title: ZX Spectrum
main.subtitle: A keyboard, a cassette and a new possibility
main.summary: An affordable British microcomputer helped make playing and programming neighbours.

cards.heading: Programming comes home
cards.text: Sinclair's ZX Spectrum arrived in 1982. Its compact keyboard and cassette-based software placed a programmable computer within reach of many British households. Games could come from a shop, a magazine listing or someone experimenting at home.

cards.heading: Constraints become a visual language
cards.text: Its characteristic colour attributes became part of a recognisable graphic style. The wider home-computer scene also supported small publishers and designers whose work did not need to begin inside a console manufacturer.

cards.heading: The household supplies a workshop
cards.text: Steve Wetherill remembered learning to program in an unheated Barnsley bedroom. His mother had bought him a Spectrum and a small television; a cassette held the assembler he needed to write code. A crash could mean rewinding and loading it again. Borrowing the family's colour set meant competing with everyone else's viewing. In his account, the route into games passed through ordinary domestic arrangements: money found for a machine, space borrowed from a household and evenings spent waiting for a tape to finish.

cards.heading: A demo travels by post
cards.text: A demonstration could travel where its maker had never worked. Wetherill recalled answering magazine advertisements by posting a cassette protected between pieces of cardboard. His scrolling platformer secured an interview at Software Projects in Liverpool in early 1984. Another candidate was Stoo Fotheringham, who later moved from programming into pixel art. Wetherill's account follows that meeting into shared accommodation and offices in a former hosiery factory. The bedroom was a starting place; a postal package opened the way to colleagues, employers and another city.

cards.heading: A rejected experiment finds work
cards.text: Bob Pape's demonstration tape carried a rejected idea as well as a job application. He had made additions to The Quill adventure system, including text compression and scrolling, but its makers were uninterested. He put those experiments alongside other work and sent them to Catalyst Coders. The tape helped him obtain the Rampage commission. Remembering it in 1997, Pape described a practical portfolio assembled from things he had already tried. An unsuccessful approach to one company became evidence of useful skills for another.

cards.heading: The bedroom leads to colleagues
cards.text: Pape remembered making Spectrum R-Type alongside programmers handling other versions in a Fareham office. Its colour also depended on a technical choice: characters moved in steps while the background scrolled by pixels. He credited Mark Jones's graphics and Rob Hylands's sound driver elsewhere in the interview. The conversion brought together distinct kinds of knowledge about the same small machine. Behind the image of the solitary bedroom programmer stood artists, specialists and fellow developers, sharing the work that turned an arcade game into a home version.

main.title: Yars' Revenge
main.subtitle: An insect against a fortress
main.summary: Yars' Revenge is Howard Scott Warshaw's single-screen shooter, published by Atari for the Atari 2600 in May 1982.

cards.heading: An insect against a fortress
cards.text: Yars' Revenge is Howard Scott Warshaw's single-screen shooter, published by Atari for the Atari 2600 in May 1982. The player controls a winged alien fighting the Qotile, an enemy protected by a wall of energy cells. Shooting the wall or eating its cells opens a route for the powerful Zorlon cannon. The small battlefield concentrates the entire struggle into a few moving pieces: a vulnerable target, a pursuing missile and the insect that must prepare its own opportunity to strike.

cards.heading: A cannon that endangers its owner
cards.text: The Zorlon cannon appears at the left edge and follows the Yar's vertical position. A successful attack therefore needs alignment followed by a quick escape from the cannon's path: its shot can destroy the player too. The colorful neutral zone offers protection from the destroyer missile, but prevents the Yar from firing. Moving between shelter and attack gives the screen a changing rhythm. Meanwhile, the Qotile can turn into a dangerous spinning swirl, making an apparently safe approach suddenly demand another decision.

cards.heading: From an arcade assignment to a new world
cards.text: Warshaw initially received an assignment to adapt the arcade game Star Castle. His work developed into a different game with its own rules and an elaborate science-fiction backstory, which accompanied the cartridge as a comic. That fiction turns the abstract shield and shifting band of color into traces of a conflict between planets. The screen remains immediately readable as a contest of movement and timing, while the illustrated story gives names and motives to the unusual shapes that Atari's hardware brings to life.

main.title: Oil Panic
main.subtitle: Oil Panic Folds Handheld Play into Two Screens
main.summary: Nintendo released Oil Panic in Japan on May 28, 1982, the first Game & Watch title in the Multi Screen line.

cards.heading: Oil Panic Folds Handheld Play into Two Screens
cards.text: Oil Panic is Nintendo's Game & Watch game released in Japan on 28 May 1982, the first in the Multi Screen line. Its folding case contains two LCD displays. The character catches falling oil on the upper screen, then empties it on the lower one while avoiding people. Watching the container's capacity and choosing when to empty it links the two displays into one task.

cards.heading: The Hinge Becomes a Rule
cards.text: The hinge allows the unit to close and protect its displays. Opened for play, it separates the action into an upper and lower area. Collecting oil and emptying the container require attention at different moments, so the player needs to shift focus between them. The physical arrangement helps make those linked jobs distinct.

cards.heading: The Character Lives Between Two Tasks
cards.text: The upper character moves beneath falling drops to fill a container. Emptying it requires judging the lower screen correctly, where a mistake can hit a person. The player must remember how much capacity remains while anticipating the next movements. Fixed LCD segments provide the possible positions; combinations of those positions create the sequence of actions the player has to follow.

cards.heading: A Portable Form That Anticipates Later Generations
cards.text: Nintendo later returned to a folding, two-screen handheld form with Nintendo DS. Its more advanced hardware supported different kinds of interaction, while sharing the practical ideas of protected displays and information divided between two surfaces. Oil Panic shows an earlier use of that physical arrangement, with the displays separating two closely connected parts of a game.

main.title: Pole Position
main.summary: Pole Position is a 1982 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.text: Pole Position is a 1982 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It was released by Atari, Inc. in North America. It was developed as a successor of Namco's earlier arcade racing electro-mechanical games, like F-1 (1976), whose designer Sho Osugi worked on Pole Position.

The game was a major commercial success in arcades. After becoming the highest-grossing arcade game of 1982 in Japan, it went on to become the most popular coin-operated arcade video game internationally in 1983. In North America, it was the highest-grossing arcade game for both 1983 and 1984 and still one of the top five in 1985.

Pole Position spawned ports, sequels, and a Saturday morning cartoon, although the cartoon has little in common with the game. The game established the conventions of the racing genre and its success inspired many imitators. Pole Position is regarded as one of the most influential video games of all time, and is considered to be the most influential racing game, as well as one of the most important titles from the golden age of arcade video games. A sequel, Pole Position II, was released in 1983 with four tracks instead of one.

main.title: Front Line
main.summary: Front Line is a 1982 run and gun video game developed and published by Taito for arcades.

cards.text: Front Line is a 1982 run and gun video game developed and published by Taito for arcades. It was one of the first overhead run and gun games, a precursor to many similarly-themed games of the mid-to-late 1980s. Front Line is controlled with a joystick, a single button, and a rotary dial that can be pushed in like a button. The single button is used to throw grenades and to enter and exit tanks, while the rotary dial aims and fires the player's gun.

The game was a commercial success in Japan, where it was the seventh highest-grossing arcade game of 1982. However, it received a mixed critical and commercial reception in Western markets, with praise for its originality but criticism for its difficulty. The game's overhead run and gun formula preceded Capcom's Commando (1985) by several years. The SNK shooters TNK III (1985) and Ikari Warriors (1986) follow conventions established by Front Line, including the vertically scrolling levels, entering/exiting tanks, and not dying when an occupied tank is destroyed.

main.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
main.subtitle: A five-week deadline and a desert legend
main.summary: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial is a 1982 adventure video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for the Atari 2600, based on the film of the same name.

cards.heading: Calling home
cards.text: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial is a 1982 adventure video game developed and published by Atari, Inc. for the Atari 2600, based on the film of the same name. The game's objective is to guide the eponymous character through various screens to collect three pieces of an interplanetary telephone that will allow him to contact his home planet.

cards.heading: Five weeks to build a game
cards.text: The game was designed by Howard Scott Warshaw, who intended it to be an innovative adaptation, but Atari held unrealistic expectations for sales based on the international box-office success of the film. Negotiations for the game rights ended in late July 1982, giving Warshaw just over five weeks to develop the game in time to meet the production schedule for the 1982 Christmas season. The final release received negative reviews and is often cited as one of the worst video games of all time, as well as one of the biggest commercial failures in video game history. It is cited as a major contributing factor to the video game crash of 1983, and has been frequently referenced and mocked in popular culture as a cautionary tale about the dangers of rushed game development and studio interference.

cards.heading: The desert legend
cards.text: In what was once deemed only an urban legend, reports from 1983 stated that as a result of overproduction and returns, unsold cartridges of E.T. were secretly buried in a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, and covered with a layer of concrete. In April 2014, diggers hired to investigate the claim confirmed that the landfill contained several E.T. cartridges, among other games.

cards.heading: What the excavation actually found
cards.text: James Heller, the former Atari manager who was in charge of the burial, was at the excavation, and admitted to the Associated Press that 728,000 cartridges of various games (not just E.T.) were buried. Marty Goldberg, co-author of the book Atari Inc.: Business Is Fun, added that the dump was in fact a clearing out of the Texas Atari manufacturing plant's unused cartridge stock of a number of titles, as well as console and computer parts. According to the 2014 documentary Atari: Game Over, only 10% of the approximately 1,300 recovered were E.T. cartridges.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1983
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 1983 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.
